examples.problem_statement:
Select the two answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole and produce completed sentences that are alike in meaning.

Biologists agree that snakes descended from lizards, but exactly where this first happened has been a matter of debate since the 1800s, when two ______ theories emerged.

A complex   B competing   C dubious   D conclusive   E contending   F irrefutable

solution.operation: Read the connector "but" joining the two halves of the sentence
solution.result: the second half must contrast in some way with the first half
solution.description: Locate the pivot word before choosing anything: "but" signals that whatever follows it stands opposed to the clause before it, so the blank has to serve that opposition.

solution.operation: Name the two sides of the contrast: agreement on the central fact (snakes descended from lizards) versus a long-standing debate over the detail (exactly where)
solution.result: the blank must emphasize the biologists' disagreement about the two theories
solution.description: Spell out what is being contrasted so the requirement on the blank becomes concrete — the word must foreground disagreement, not merely describe a theory.

solution.operation: Test "competing" (B) and "contending" (E) against that requirement
solution.result: both imply the two theories are what the long-running debate has centered upon
solution.description: Check the candidate pair: each word casts the two theories as rivals, which is exactly the disagreement the sentence needs, and the two are alike in meaning as the question type demands.

solution.operation: Test the other synonym pair, "conclusive" (D) and "irrefutable" (F)
solution.result: roughly synonymous, but neither suggests a matter worthy of a long-running debate
solution.description: Reject this pair on sense rather than on form: theories described as settled beyond dispute could not have fueled debate since the 1800s.

solution.operation: Test the leftover choices "dubious" (C) and "complex" (A)
solution.result: neither has a near-synonym among the choices; "dubious" would not explain why the two theories triggered the debate, and "complex" does not foreground the biologists' disagreement
solution.description: Eliminate the singletons: sentence equivalence requires a matching pair, and on meaning alone each of these fails to account for the debate the sentence describes.

solution.operation: Take the surviving pair
solution.result: competing (Choice B) and contending (Choice E)
solution.description: Commit to the one pair that both matches in meaning and satisfies the contrast set up by "but".

examples.answer: Choice B: competing; AND Choice E: contending

key_reminders: "but" marks a contrast, so the blank must carry the opposition between the two clauses.
Sentence equivalence needs two choices that are alike in meaning AND fit the sentence — a synonym pair that misfits the sense is still wrong.
A choice with no near-synonym among the options cannot be part of the answer.
common_mistakes: Picking "conclusive" and "irrefutable" just because they form a clean synonym pair, without checking that settled theories could not sustain a debate since the 1800s.
Choosing "complex" because it plausibly describes a theory, ignoring that it has no partner among the choices and does not express disagreement.

examples.problem_statement:
Mycenaean Vase. Museum A will display only objects that are undamaged and that have been definitively proven to be authentic. Doubts have been raised about the origins of a supposedly Mycenaean vase currently on display in the museum's antiquities wing. The only way to establish this vase's authenticity would be to pulverize it, then subject the dust to spectroscopic analysis.

The claims above, if true, most strongly support which of the following conclusions?

(A) Authentic Mycenaean vases are valuable and rare.
(B) Museum A was not sufficiently diligent in establishing the authenticity of the vase before displaying it.
(C) The vase in question will no longer be displayed in Museum A.
(D) Spectroscopic analysis is the only method used by Museum A to establish the authenticity of objects.
(E) Many of the world's museums unknowingly display forgeries.

solution.operation: Identify the question from the stem wording "most strongly support which of the following conclusions"
solution.result: an Inference question — the conclusion sits in the answer choices, not in the argument
solution.description: "Strongly support" alone could mean Inference or Strengthen; the phrase "which of the following conclusions" settles it, because it places the conclusion among the answers.

solution.operation: Deconstruct claim 1: Museum A displays only objects that are undamaged and definitively proven authentic
solution.result: Mus: only perfect, authenticated objects
solution.description: Record the museum's display rule as a fact — both conditions, undamaged and authenticated, must hold for anything on display.

solution.operation: Deconstruct claim 2: doubts have been raised about the origins of the vase now on display
solution.result: Doubts about Myc vase
solution.description: Note the second fact: the vase's authenticity is currently unsettled.

solution.operation: Deconstruct claim 3: the only way to establish authenticity is to pulverize the vase and analyze the dust
solution.result: To authenticate, the museum must destroy the vase
solution.description: Capture the trap built into the third fact — the sole authentication route destroys the object it would authenticate.

solution.operation: State the goal by chaining the three facts
solution.result: they cannot display a vase not proven authentic, and cannot display a pulverized one — so it cannot be displayed at all
solution.description: An Inference answer must be provable from the given information; combining the display rule with the destructive test forces the outcome before you read the choices.

solution.operation: Test (A): authentic Mycenaean vases are valuable and rare
solution.result: eliminated — might be true, but unprovable from the argument
solution.description: Value and rarity are never mentioned, and outside plausibility is not proof, so this fails the must-be-true standard.

solution.operation: Test (B): the museum was not sufficiently diligent before displaying the vase
solution.result: tempting but eliminated — it is a value judgment, not something the facts establish
solution.description: It feels reasonable to ask why an unauthenticated vase was on display, but "not sufficiently diligent" is a judgment the argument never supports.

solution.operation: Test (C): the vase will no longer be displayed in Museum A
solution.result: provable — this matches the chain built in step 5
solution.description: Either they leave it unauthenticated (barred by the display rule) or they authenticate it by destroying it (nothing left to display); either way it comes off display, and unlike (B) this rests on logic rather than judgment.

solution.operation: Test (D) and (E): spectroscopy is the museum's only authentication method; many museums unknowingly display forgeries
solution.result: both eliminated — overreach beyond the given information
solution.description: The argument requires spectroscopy only for this vase, leaving other methods possible for other objects, and it describes one museum and one object, never many of the world's museums.

key_reminders: On an Inference question the correct answer must be provable from the stated facts alone.
"Which of the following conclusions" means the argument has no conclusion — it is in the answer choices.
A conditional rule plus a fact that makes the condition unsatisfiable forces the negative outcome.
common_mistakes: Choosing (B) because blaming the museum feels reasonable — it is a value judgment the three claims do not prove.
Choosing (D) by generalizing "the only way to establish this vase's authenticity" into the museum's only method for every object.

concept.technique_name: three-blank text completion by easiest-blank-first anchoring

examples.problem_statement:
Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices. Fill all blanks in the way that best completes the text.

When the normally (i) ______ film director was interviewed, it was only the topic of her next movie that (ii) ______ her flow of words. Her (iii) ______ on that subject suggested that it was an unwelcome one.

Blank (i): A assiduous, B loquacious, C diffident
Blank (ii): D diverted, E stanched, F accentuated
Blank (iii): G taciturnity, H alacrity, I rhapsody

solution.operation: Start at Blank (iii), where the sentence supplies its own gloss: the director's reaction shows the topic is unwelcome
solution.result: Blank (iii) must name a reaction that signals the subject is unwelcome
solution.description: Anchor on the blank whose meaning the sentence states outright, so the other two can be resolved against a fixed point.

solution.operation: Test "alacrity" (H) and "rhapsody" (I) for Blank (iii)
solution.result: both eliminated — each indicates excitement or eagerness to talk about the topic
solution.description: Eagerness contradicts the sentence's own statement that the subject is unwelcome, so both choices are implausible.

solution.operation: Take "taciturnity" (G) for Blank (iii)
solution.result: taciturnity indicates unwillingness or reserve about speaking — the correct choice
solution.description: The surviving word denotes silence or reserve, exactly the reaction that would mark the topic as unwelcome.

solution.operation: Fill Blank (i), which must contrast with that taciturnity because it describes the director's normal conversational style
solution.result: loquacious (B); "diffident" means reserved and "assiduous" means diligent, so neither supplies the contrast
solution.description: The word "normally" sets the usual behavior against the exceptional reaction, so Blank (i) needs a ready willingness to converse — "diffident" would echo taciturnity instead of opposing it, and "assiduous" is off the axis of talkativeness entirely.

solution.operation: Fill Blank (ii), the verb describing what the unwelcome topic did to the flow of words of a normally talkative person
solution.result: stanched (E); "accentuated" indicates the opposite, and "diverted" implies a change of topic unsupported by the passage
solution.description: The topic checked her conversation, so the verb must stop the flow — "accentuated" would increase it, and "diverted" smuggles in a redirection the rest of the sentence never mentions.

solution.operation: Assemble the three choices
solution.result: loquacious (B), stanched (E), taciturnity (G)
solution.description: Read the completed sentence back to confirm the normally talkative director fell silent on the one unwelcome subject.

examples.answer: Choice B: loquacious; Choice E: stanched; Choice G: taciturnity

key_reminders: Fill the blank the sentence explains first, then use it as the anchor for the others.
"Normally" signals a contrast between habitual behavior and the exceptional reaction described.
Reject a choice that adds information the rest of the sentence does not support.
common_mistakes: Working Blank (i) first, before the sentence's own gloss on Blank (iii) has fixed the direction of the contrast.
Choosing "diverted" for Blank (ii) because interrupting speech sounds plausible, though nothing in the sentence indicates a change of topic.
Reading "diffident" as merely quiet-mannered and letting it stand as the director's normal style, which erases the required contrast with taciturnity.

concept.technique_name: All from 9 and the last from 10 (Nikhilam) subtraction

examples.problem_statement: Using the Vedic subtraction technique built on the sutra "All from 9 and the last from 10", evaluate 459876 - 389924. Work column by column from right to left across all 6 columns, using ordinary subtraction where the minuend digit is larger and the complement rule where it is not. Reproduce the method step by step and state the final result.

solution.operation: Scan right to left; where the minuend digit exceeds the subtrahend digit (6 > 4, 7 > 2) subtract normally: 6 - 4 and 7 - 2
solution.result: units digit = 2, tens digit = 5
solution.description: Begin at the right and handle the easy columns first — when the top digit is the larger one, no complement is needed and plain subtraction gives the digit.

solution.operation: At the hundreds column the minuend digit is smaller (8 < 9), so apply the sutra: 10 - (9 - 8)
solution.result: hundreds digit = 9
solution.description: This is the column that triggers the rule: take the shortfall of the minuend below the subtrahend, then complete it from 10 to get the digit.

solution.operation: At the thousands column the digits are equal (9 and 9), so subtract the difference from 9: 9 - (9 - 9)
solution.result: thousands digit = 9
solution.description: An equal-digit column sits inside the complement run, so it takes the "all from 9" form rather than plain subtraction, and the zero difference leaves 9.

solution.operation: At the ten thousands column the minuend digit is again smaller (5 < 8): 9 - (8 - 5)
solution.result: ten thousands digit = 6
solution.description: Another shortfall column, still inside the complement run, so subtract the difference from 9 rather than from 10.

solution.operation: At the hundred thousands column the minuend digit is larger (4 > 3) but a complement was used in the previous column, so subtract an extra 1: 4 - 3 - 1
solution.result: hundred thousands digit = 0
solution.description: Pay back the borrow created by the complement run — the leading column returns to normal subtraction but must give up one unit to the column on its right.

solution.operation: Read the digits back from the hundred thousands column down to the units: 0, 6, 9, 9, 5, 2
solution.description: Assemble the per-column digits in place-value order to state the difference.

examples.answer: 459876 - 389924 = 069952 using Vedic subtraction with complement method

key_reminders: Work right to left, deciding column by column whether the minuend digit is larger.
Where the minuend digit is smaller, the first such column completes from 10 and the columns continuing the run take all from 9.
A column that follows a complement column loses an extra 1 when it reverts to normal subtraction.
common_mistakes: Treating the 9 - 9 thousands column as plain subtraction and writing 0 instead of the 9 the complement run requires.
Forgetting the extra -1 in the leading 4 - 3 column, which turns the leading digit into 1 and inflates the answer by 100000.

concept.technique_name: three-blank text completion by internal-contrast cues

examples.problem_statement:
Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices. Fill all blanks in the way that best completes the text.

The most striking thing about the politician is how often his politics have been (i) ______ rather than ideological, as he adapts his political positions at any particular moment to the political realities that constrain him. He does not, however, piously (ii) ______ political principles only to betray them in practice. Rather, he attempts in subtle ways to balance his political self-interest with a (iii) ______, viewing himself as an instrument of some unchanging higher purpose.

Blank (i): A quixotic, B self-righteous, C strategic
Blank (ii): D brandish, E flout, F follow
Blank (iii): G profound cynicism, H deeply felt moral code, I thoroughgoing pragmatism

solution.operation: Fill Blank (i) from the clause "adapts his political positions ... to the political realities that constrain him", and check it against "rather than ideological"
solution.result: strategic (C) — the only choice that also provides the required contrast with "ideological"
solution.description: The sentence both defines the blank and opposes it to "ideological", so the word must name politics driven by circumstance rather than doctrine; "strategic" is the only choice that does both.

solution.operation: Fill Blank (ii) with the verb that a politician might do piously to political principles before betraying them in practice
solution.result: brandish (D)
solution.description: The adverb "piously" and the follow-on "only to betray them in practice" require a showy public display of principles, which is what brandishing them means.

solution.operation: Test the rival choices "flout" (E) and "follow" (F) for Blank (ii)
solution.result: both eliminated — flouting is not pious, and following principles does not fit with betraying them in practice
solution.description: Check each against the two cues separately: "flout" fails the "piously" cue, and "follow" contradicts the betrayal that the sentence says comes next.

solution.operation: Fill Blank (iii) with something that must be balanced against "political self-interest" and embraced in service of an "unchanging higher purpose"
solution.result: deeply felt moral code (H) — the only viable choice
solution.description: The blank sits on the opposite side of a balance from self-interest and is glossed by the higher-purpose clause, so it needs a genuine moral commitment; cynicism and pragmatism would sit with self-interest, not against it.

solution.operation: Assemble the three choices
solution.result: strategic (C), brandish (D), deeply felt moral code (H)
solution.description: Read the completed passage back: a politician who is strategic rather than ideological, who does not merely parade principles, and who still answers to a genuine moral code.

examples.answer: Choice C: strategic; Choice D: brandish; Choice H: deeply felt moral code

key_reminders: "Rather than" marks a contrast: the blank must oppose the word on the other side of the phrase.
"However" and "Rather" reverse the direction of the argument between sentences — track that reversal when filling the later blanks.
A blank balanced against a stated quality must contrast with it, not restate it.
common_mistakes: Choosing "flout" for Blank (ii) because the sentence is about betrayal, overlooking that "piously" demands a display of devotion, not defiance.
Choosing "thoroughgoing pragmatism" for Blank (iii) by carrying over the adaptability of Blank (i), when the blank must be balanced against self-interest rather than aligned with it.
